findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement submitted late to audit, creating resource and schedule pressures
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement was not provided with the draft financial statements and submitted late in the audit process, creating additional resourcing and timetable pressures. The auditor expects the AGS to be prepared and submitted alongside draft accounts in future years to support timely and efficient audit completion.
findings.matters: Timely submission of audit documentation is essential for maintaining schedule integrity and controlling audit costs. Late submissions can cascade delays in publication of audited accounts.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Annual Governance Statement (AGS) was not provided alongside the draft financial statements and was submitted at a late stage of the audit process. This created additional resourcing and timetable pressures in completing the necessary audit work on the AGS before the North Wales CJC's consideration of the financial statements.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: First full year audit of North Wales CJC required more work than original estimate due to transition complexity
findings.detail: The 2025-26 audit was the first full year following transfer of NWEAB arrangements to the CJC on 1 April 2025. The audit required additional work beyond the original fee estimate of £34,832 to understand new governance arrangements, reporting requirements, accounting treatments, and to audit opening balances transferred to the entity. The final fee is to be agreed with the Statutory Finance Officer.
findings.matters: Finance directors managing transitions of public bodies need visibility of audit cost implications when establishing new accounting systems and governance arrangements, which can significantly exceed initial estimates.
findings.figures: £34,832 original estimate
findings.quote: As this was the first year that the North Wales CJC prepared a full set of financial statements following the transfer of the North Wales Economic Ambition Board arrangements on 1 April 2025, the audit involved more work than originally anticipated. Additional work was required to understand and evaluate the new governance arrangements, reporting requirements, accounting treatments, and the opening balances transferred to the CJC.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: Welsh Government did not confirm accounting treatment for Parc Bryn Cegin collaborative arrangement
findings.detail: The auditor identified uncertainty regarding the accounting treatment of the CJC's collaborative agreement with Welsh Government for Parc Bryn Cegin, where Welsh Government provides land and the CJC provides funding. Welsh Government did not respond to clarification requests before the audit concluded, leaving the treatment unresolved. The auditor was unable to fully conclude on its appropriateness, though notes potential impact is not expected to be material to 2025-26 accounts. The matter is flagged for monitoring as the arrangement develops.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need visibility of significant material-by-nature transactions with key funders where accounting treatment is unresolved, as this affects balance sheet presentation and creates uncertainty for future reporting.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: During the audit, we identified uncertainty regarding the accounting treatment of the collaborative agreement with Welsh Government for Parc Bryn Cegin. We sought clarification from Welsh Government on the appropriate accounting treatment; however, a response had not been received before completion of our audit work. Consequently, we were unable to conclude fully on whether the treatment adopted by the CJC is appropriate.

findings.detail: The CJC decided to use 80% of estimated usable reserves (£839,850) combined with a levy increase to balance the budget. This was chosen as a middle ground: a pure freeze would require £1,148,650 in reserves (a £308,799 shortfall), while using no reserves would require a 113% increase.
findings.matters: The levy is the primary recurring funding source for the CJC, and this increase directly impacts the budgets of all six constituent councils for 2027/28 and signals their exposure to further increases in following years
findings.figures: 42% levy increase 2027/28; 80% of £839,850 reserves; alternative option required 113% increase
findings.quote: As can be seen, it would mean an increase in levy on the constituent authorities of 42% in 2027/28 compared to 2026/27.

findings.headline: 160MW Alaw Môn Solar Farm granted planning permission in August 2025; major renewable energy infrastructure investment approved
findings.detail: One commercial-scale renewable energy development was approved in the monitoring period: Alaw Môn Solar Farm (Enso Energy, 160MW). This represents significant capital investment in renewable energy infrastructure. Multiple other renewable projects remain in progress, including Morlais tidal arrays (240MW), Parc Solar Traffwll (35MW), and Porth Wen Solar Farm (49.99MW, now operational).
findings.matters: Major renewable energy project approval signals ongoing capital investment and economic activity in the area. Permitted renewable schemes total 3,421.60 GWh potential, supporting future business rates and employment from green energy sectors.
findings.figures: 160MW capacity approved; total permitted schemes potential 3,421.60 GWh
findings.quote: In this monitoring period one new renewable energy commercial scale development was granted planning permission, namely Alaw Môn Solar Farm (Enso Energy) (160MW) (permission given in August 2025).

findings.headline: Employment land take-up at 5.189 hectares against annual target of 6.9 hectares in 2025/26
findings.detail: Employment land permissions fall 1.7 hectares short of the annual target in the monitoring period. Cumulative take-up since plan adoption totals 22.099 hectares. The council acknowledges that 'the economic climate is significantly different to when the Plan was adopted, and it is considered that this has had a considerable impact on the take up of employment land.'
findings.matters: Employment land take-up below target indicates slower than forecast business investment and economic growth in the area, directly affecting future business rates income and employment prospects. Underperformance reflects weaker economic conditions than plan assumptions.
findings.figures: 5.189 hectares achieved vs 6.9 hectares annual target (-1.7 hectares); cumulative 22.099 hectares since 2017 adoption
findings.quote: In Gwynedd, 5.189ha of land has received permission for employment use on safeguarded employment sites during the eighth Annual Monitoring Report period (AMB8). Target: 6.9 ha employment land on safeguarded sites taken up per annum in Gwynedd

findings.headline: 91 affordable housing units completed (77% of 118 total completions); 80% of new permissions meeting threshold included affordable housing
findings.detail: Affordable housing delivery is performing strongly. In 2025/26, 91 of 118 completed units were affordable (77%). For new permissions, 145 of 182 units meeting the affordable housing contribution threshold were granted with affordable housing conditions or legal agreements (80% compliance). Since plan adoption, 639 of 1,159 units completed have been affordable (55.1%).
findings.matters: Strong affordable housing delivery indicates the council is effectively implementing housing policy objectives, maintaining workforce stability, and potentially supporting community sustainability. This positive performance amid overall housing shortfall suggests policy is working in the affordable segment.
findings.figures: 91 affordable units of 118 completions (77%); 145 of 182 units meeting threshold (80%); cumulative 639 of 1,159 since adoption (55.1%)
findings.quote: 91 affordable housing units completed in 2025/26 which is 77% of the total completions for this year.

findings.headline: Wylfa Newydd nuclear power station Development Consent Order withdrawn by Horizon Nuclear Power in January 2021
findings.detail: The proposed nuclear power station project, which had been subject to a Development Consent Order application, has been terminated. Horizon Nuclear Power withdrew the application due to lack of investor funding and absence of government funding policy support. No associated development has commenced and the infrastructure permissions (A5025 improvements granted in 2018) remain unexercised.
findings.matters: A major planned capital investment and economic driver has been eliminated, removing expected future jobs, investment, and economic growth. A lender would need to understand how the loss of this significant infrastructure project affects broader regional economic development plans and the council's future revenue prospects.
findings.figures: None quantified in document regarding scale of cancelled investment
findings.quote: On the 27th of January 2021 the Development Order Application was withdrawn by Horizon Nuclear Power. The application was withdrawn due to the lack of investors in the project and the lack of a new funding policy from the Government.

findings.headline: 118 homes completed in 2025/26 against annual requirement of 247 units, a shortfall of 52.2%
findings.detail: Gwynedd completed 118 housing units in the monitoring period, 129 units below the annual average requirement of 247 and 107 units below the forecast trajectory of 225. Cumulative completions since plan adoption in 2017 stand at 2,805 units against a trajectory target of 3,712 units (24.4% below). This represents structural under-delivery of housing throughout the plan period.
findings.matters: Housing delivery below target constrains local economic growth prospects, affects council tax and business rates base growth, and signals whether the council is meeting national housing supply targets. Persistent shortfall indicates either planning constraints or weaker than forecast economic demand.
findings.figures: 118 completed vs 247 required (-52.2%); vs 225 trajectory (-47.6%); cumulative 2,805 vs 3,712 targeted (-24.4%)
findings.quote: In this AMR period, it is noted that 118 units have been completed in the Gwynedd Planning Authority area. The Annual Average Requirement is 247 units for Gwynedd alone (therefore 129 fewer units or -52.2%)

findings.headline: Total debt £81.0m against capital financing requirement of £192.9m forecast for 31 March 2027; financing costs rising to 2.7% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: Total external debt (including PFI and leases) was £81.0m at end of August 2026, against a capital financing requirement forecast of £192.9m at 31 March 2027, providing £111.9m headroom. The council is compliant with its authorised limit of £200m and operational boundary of £190m. Financing costs are forecast at £9.9m for 2026/27 (2.7% of net revenue stream), up from 2.4% actual in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Demonstrates prudential code compliance and debt headroom; rising financing cost ratio (2.4% to 2.7%) indicates increasing capital servicing burden relative to revenue income; lenders track trajectory of this ratio
findings.figures: Total debt £81.0m; CFR £192.9m forecast; Authorised limit £200m; Operational boundary £190m; Financing costs 2.7% 2026/27 (vs 2.4% 2025/26)
findings.quote: Statutory guidance is that debt should remain below the capital financing requirement, except in the short-term. The Council has complied and expects to continue to comply with this requirement in the medium term

findings.headline: Capital spending at 15% of full-year programme by end of August; consistent with prior two years' delivery rate
findings.detail: By 31 August 2026, the council had spent £19.072m of its £123.456m full-year capital programme. This 15% spend rate matches the position achieved at the same point in both 2025/26 and 2024/25, indicating a consistent capital delivery profile.
findings.matters: Consistent spending trajectory supports year-end forecast accuracy; identifies whether council is accelerating or falling behind scheduled delivery
findings.figures: £19.072m spent in 5 months; 15% of £123.456m programme; same 15% achieved in 2024/25 and 2025/26 at same point
findings.quote: The percentage spent this year (15%) is similar to the position this time last year (amount spent in 5 months in 2025/26 was 15%) and two years ago (amount spent in 5 months in 2024/25 was 15%).

findings.headline: Bangor Health and Wellbeing Centre scheme adjusted with expenditure profile now extending beyond three-year capital programme forecast
findings.detail: The council has adjusted the Bangor Health and Wellbeing Centre scheme (part of Asset Management Plan), reducing its capital fund contribution by £350,000. The adjustment means the scheme now extends beyond the three-year programme period shown, indicating further expenditure in later years not yet detailed in the current capital forecast.
findings.matters: Scheme timing adjustment may signal cost or delivery challenges; defers capital requirement but extends overall commitment; affects medium-term financial planning
findings.figures: £350,000 reduction in capital fund for the scheme in 2026/27
findings.quote: Adjustment to the Bangor Health and Wellbeing Centre scheme (part of the Asset Management Plan) where the adjusted profile goes beyond the three years shown in the current Capital Programme

findings.headline: £12.0m of capital expenditure re-profiled from 2026/27 to later years; council states no loss of grant funding but services must cope longer with existing unimproved assets
findings.detail: Capital schemes worth £12.0m have been moved from 2026/27 into 2027/28 and 2028/29. Slippage includes £5.904m schools projects, £2.854m Levelling Up Fund, £1.058m Coastal Risk and Flood Prevention Plans, and others. The council confirms grant funding was not lost, but acknowledges delays mean services must continue operating with existing unimproved facilities.
findings.matters: Delays in capital delivery postpone service improvements and affect asset condition; finance directors track whether funding remains available when schemes are deferred
findings.figures: £12.0m re-profiled from 2026/27; £5.904m schools; £2.854m Levelling Up Fund; £1.058m Coastal schemes
findings.quote: An additional £12.0m of proposed expenditure has been re-profiled from 2026/27 to 2027/28 and 2028/29, but no loss of funding was caused to the Council where schemes have slipped. The delay prior to implementing these schemes can mean that the services must cope for longer with the existing unimproved assets.

findings.headline: Council approved additional borrowing of £846,000 for renewal of vehicles and equipment in highways and environment departments
findings.detail: The council has increased planned borrowing by £846,000 to fund vehicles and equipment renewal. This represents a deliberate capital financing choice to debt-finance fleet replacement in Highways, Engineering and Consultancy and Environment departments.
findings.matters: Increases council debt position and future revenue servicing costs; demonstrates continued access to borrowing markets for specific asset classes
findings.figures: £846,000 additional borrowing approved
findings.quote: Renewal of Vehicles and Equipment by borrowing (Highways, Engineering and Consultancy; Environment Departments). 846

findings.headline: Renewal and other reserves increased by £13.329m to fund capital spending, dominated by £12.4m additional draw from Council Tax Premium Fund for housing schemes
findings.detail: The council is drawing £13.329m more from renewal and other reserves than in the original budget, a shift in financing strategy. The largest single item is £12.4m additional contribution from the Council Tax Premium Fund towards housing strategy schemes. Additional movements include £794k vehicle and equipment renewals. This represents the second-largest source of new financing after grants.
findings.matters: Material reserve drawdown to avoid borrowing reduces contingency flexibility and signals asset investment priority; lenders track reserve sustainability and depletion rates
findings.figures: £13.329m total increase in reserve use; £12.4m from Council Tax Premium Fund; £794k vehicle renewals
findings.quote: Adjustment to the contribution from the Council Tax Premium Fund towards the Housing Strategy schemes (Housing and Property Department). 12,400

findings.headline: Council attracted additional grants of £66.509m since original budget, with largest awards being £24.325m New Local Growth Fund and £16.365m for Ysgol Bontnewydd school project
findings.detail: The council has successfully secured significant external funding beyond the original budget. After adjustments and withdrawals, grants and contributions have increased by £64.980m. Major grants include £24.325m New Local Growth Fund (for distribution across north Wales), £16.365m Sustainable Schools Challenge and Childcare Grant for Ysgol Bontnewydd, £11.648m Shared Prosperity Fund, and £4.260m Active Travel and Safe Routes grants. This is the largest single source of financing change in the revised programme.
findings.matters: Material reduction in reliance on council resources and borrowing; successful grant capture affects debt profile and cash flow; peer councils would watch how this council executes bids
findings.figures: £66.509m total additional grants; £64.980m net increase in programme; £24.325m, £16.365m, £11.648m individual largest grants
findings.quote: Since setting the original budget, the Council succeeded in attracting additional grants totalling £66.509m, the largest of which are listed below. Several additional adjustments, including reductions on schemes that were below the original objective or withdrawals of grants, bring the total movement to £64.980m

findings.headline: Sustainable schools modernization programme enabled with £6.86M approved; further £4.11M conditional pending detailed prioritization work
findings.detail: Following adoption of a new Schools Strategy in February 2026, the council is approving £6.86M for the first phase of a sustainable schools rolling programme as 35% match funding to attract 65% Welsh Government grant. A further £4.11M is being earmarked for either additional schools modernization or responding to traffic safety issues at secondary school sites, with exact allocation to be determined following departmental scoping work. Final prioritization is being delegated to the Chief Executive.
findings.matters: Significant capital investment in school estate is being enabled, but governance is being deferred pending further analysis. The final allocation between competing education priorities (modernization vs. traffic safety) remains unconfirmed, indicating either incomplete options appraisal or resource constraint.
findings.figures: £6.86M first phase, £4.11M second phase pending prioritization, £1.7M for traffic safety (departmental bid)
findings.quote: a reorganisation and modernisation plan would need to secure a budget of around £6.86M as 35% match funding to attract a Welsh Government grant of 65%.

findings.headline: Ysgol Bontnewydd project cost overrun to £17.67M, council contribution of £583k approved with Welsh Government funding 97%
findings.detail: Welsh Government announced £15M full funding for an innovative new school at Ysgol Bontnewydd; project costs have risen to £17.67M. The council is approving a contribution of £583k (3% of total cost), with Welsh Government now funding 97%. Cost increases have been driven by inflation over an extended timeline and higher-than-expected costs for temporary school provision during construction.
findings.matters: Cost inflation on externally-funded projects still requires council match funding contributions to increase. The 97% grant covers most cost overruns but the council exposure has risen, illustrating the dependency on Welsh Government grants and the risk to match funding requirements.
findings.figures: Original Welsh Government grant £15M, actual scheme cost £17.67M, council contribution £583k, Welsh Government funding 97%
findings.quote: The cost of the scheme has now risen to £17.67M, which is higher than what was agreed and the total amount the Government is able to fund. Gwynedd needs to contribute £583,000 to be able to proceed

findings.headline: £3.5M capital funding de-committed from Health and Care Hub as partners proceed with smaller scheme without council participation
findings.detail: The Health and Care Hub project is being withdrawn as a council investment. The health board and housing association are continuing with a smaller scheme that does not include the council's planned participation. The £3.5M earmarked for this project is being de-committed. The council notes that while demography suggests future care development needs, no plans are currently sufficiently mature to commit to, with future needs to be reconsidered in a full Asset Plan review in 2029.
findings.matters: A major strategic capital project being withdrawn signals either partnership or delivery challenges. The release of funding is material to resource availability, but the underlying issue — council capital investment needs in social care infrastructure — remains unresolved.
findings.figures: £3.5M de-committed
findings.quote: it is recommended that the £3.5M capital resources earmarked for the scheme be de-committed. Any future plans and needs would be considered in a full review of the Asset Plan in 2029.

findings.headline: North Promenade flood prevention scheme cost estimate escalates from £23M to £35M, requiring additional council contribution of £1.49M
findings.detail: The North Promenade flood prevention scheme in Barmouth, protecting over 700 homes from coastal flooding, was initially estimated at £23M. Following further development work, the estimated cost has risen to approximately £35M. The council provides a 15% contribution, now estimated at £5.25M. With £3.76M already in the Asset Plan, a further £1.49M is required and being approved.
findings.matters: Major infrastructure cost escalation signals planning or market pressures and affects financial capacity. A 52% increase in scheme cost from initial estimate is material for forward planning and signals risk in other infrastructure projects.
findings.figures: Original estimate £23M, revised estimate £35M, council 15% contribution £5.25M, additional funding needed £1.49M
findings.quote: the likely cost appears to be much higher and closer to £35M. While this work is ongoing and the exact figure is not final, we need to prepare for costs significantly higher than the original £23M.

findings.headline: Council identifies £16M in additional capital resources but faces £3.76M funding shortfall against identified spending needs of £19.76M
findings.detail: Since approving the 2024-2034 Asset Plan, Gwynedd has received capital grants, receipts, and released £3.5M through de-committing the Health and Care Hub project, totalling £16M. However, requested spending across education and flood prevention projects totals £19.76M. The council cannot fund all identified schemes and must prioritise.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand the adequacy of capital resources identified, the scale of unmet needs, and how the council's forward asset planning handles trade-offs between competing priorities.
findings.figures: £16M available, £19.76M demanded, £3.76M shortfall
findings.quote: Given that there is currently £16M of additional resource available, it is not possible to fund everything and therefore, there will be a need to prioritise.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Economic Well-being Sub-committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue and Capital Position - End of July 2026 Review
findings.headline: Portfolio Management Office recorded £680,896 underspend, with £586,668 in staff costs shifted to project-level and grant funding.
findings.detail: £348,000 of staff costs are now funded by Ambition North Wales's Growth Deal projects, £121,000 by grants (Local Area Energy Plan and Shared Prosperity Fund), and vacant posts contributed over £60,000. This shows flexible funding models but also indicates staffing gaps during the year.
findings.matters: Reveals how staffing is actually distributed across projects rather than held at PMO level; peer councils track whether delivery capacity was fully deployed.
findings.figures: £680,896 PMO underspend; £586,668 employee expenditure variance; £348,000 Ambition North Wales funding; £121,000 grant funding; ~£60,000 vacancies
findings.quote: The underspend on the employee expenditure heading is £586,668 and this is due to some staff costs that were included within the core budget were subsequently funded by other sources. Around £348,000 of the underspend is due to staff that are now funded by Ambition North Wales's Growth Deal projects... These grants were therefore used to fund staff costs, which together contribute to around £121,000 of the underspend. Vacant posts during the year also led to a further underspend of over £60,000 in employee expenditure.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Economic Well-being Sub-committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue and Capital Position - End of July 2026 Review
findings.headline: Investment Zone achieving neutral budget position by using £227,589 of interest income alongside £200,000 grant allocation.
findings.detail: Interest on retained grant balances is being deployed to bridge the gap between allocated funding and forecast expenditure, achieving a neutral year-end position. This approach is explicitly described as temporary; the CJC notes that interest income will decline as cash outflows from grant distribution accelerate.
findings.matters: The underlying cost structure exceeds sustainable grant funding; reliance on interest income is time-limited and signals an emerging funding gap as balances decline.
findings.figures: £227,589 interest income used; £200,000 annual grant allocation
findings.quote: In order to leave a neutral position for the Investment Zone, interest from the Investment Zone grant balances of £227,589 will be used, in addition to the £200,000 grant allocation. The use of interest is a temporary arrangement as the cash outflows from distributing the Investment Zone grant will reduce the interest income.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Economic Well-being Sub-committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue and Capital Position - End of July 2026 Review
findings.headline: Growth Deal revenue budget forecast to underspend by £288,174 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Underspend is primarily from vacant posts and staff costs being funded from other sources, including Ambition North Wales projects, Local Area Energy Plan and Shared Prosperity Fund grants. The underspend will be carried forward to fund future budgets and reduce future partner contribution increases.
findings.matters: Demonstrates budget control and signals potential reduction in future funding pressures from partner councils.
findings.figures: £288,174 underspend
findings.quote: It is estimated that the net out-turn position at the end of the 2026/27 financial year will be an underspend of £288,174. This is mainly due to underspends in employee expenditure, additional government roles, accountable body support services and external legal, finance and procurement support. An underspend at the end of the financial year will be used to fund future budgets and reduce any increases in future partner contributions.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Economic Well-being Sub-committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue and Capital Position - End of July 2026 Review
findings.headline: Growth Deal capital expenditure forecast at £51.26m against approved budget of £67.07m, a reduction of £15.81m due to project slippage.
findings.detail: Capital spending is expected to underspend by £15.81m (23.6%) in 2026/27. Although the Business Gateway project introduction and brought-forward Reserve List projects have partially offset the slippage, project delivery delays remain substantial.
findings.matters: Material capital variance signals delivery risk; lenders and peer finance directors track whether councils are executing capital programmes as planned.
findings.figures: £51.26m forecast; £67.07m approved budget; £15.81m reduction
findings.quote: There is a net reduction of £15.81m in the anticipated expenditure for 2026/27 and this is due to slippage on projects. However, the introduction of the Business Gateway project in the capital profile and the brought forward expenditure on the Reserve List projects have reduced the slippage.

findings.headline: Ombudsman complaints increased despite overall formal complaint numbers falling
findings.detail: The council saw formal complaints decrease overall, but those escalated to Ombudsman increased. This suggests that complaints being made are either more serious or less resolvable through council processes.
findings.matters: Rising Ombudsman escalations can indicate either deteriorating service quality or poor complaint resolution, both affecting reputation and potentially generating costs.
findings.figures: No specific complaint numbers provided
findings.quote: The number of Valid Formal Complaints has decreased this year compared to last year, but those that have gone to the Ombudsman have increased.

findings.headline: Staff satisfaction declined in 2024 during period of fiscal uncertainty and political change
findings.detail: The 2024 Llais Staff Survey recorded declines in satisfaction levels across most questions during a period that included fiscal uncertainty, political changes, and workplace reorganisation. However, key satisfaction metrics remained relatively high (80% for council being a good place to work; 87% for motivation).
findings.matters: Declining staff morale during budget pressure can signal workforce instability. Experience loss or departures among skilled staff during financial difficulty can affect service delivery and continuity.
findings.figures: 80% satisfaction for 'Council is a good place to work'; 87% for motivation. Overall satisfaction decreased from prior year.
findings.quote: there has been a slight decrease in the level of staff satisfaction in response to most of the questions

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rates are below target; internal review underway to improve collection
findings.detail: Governance statement confirms an internal review has been initiated specifically to improve Council Tax collection arrangements. The decision to review and introduce improvement actions indicates current collection rates are not meeting targets.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a material income source for local authorities. Below-target collection directly affects revenue available for services and budget balance, particularly significant given existing overspend problems.
findings.figures: No specific collection rate figures disclosed
findings.quote: An internal review is underway to improve our Council Tax collection arrangements, and actions have been introduced to increase collection rates in the future.

findings.headline: Council governance statement warns future funds may be insufficient to address budget shortfall
findings.detail: The Finance section acknowledges that with continuing pressure to find savings combined with increasing service demand, a structural deficit situation could emerge without identified funding solutions. This is explicit language about potential insolvency risk.
findings.matters: This is direct acknowledgment of potential solvency and deficit risk. A lender needs to know if a council projects structural deficits without a path to balance.
findings.figures: None specific to future years
findings.quote: as the need to find savings continues, and demand for services increases, a situation can be envisaged where there are insufficient funds in the future to address the budget shortfall.

findings.headline: Gwynedd overspent in 2024/25 and 2025/26; 2027/28 budget setting will be challenging
findings.detail: The council has recorded actual overspends in two consecutive years and explicitly identifies 2027/28 budget setting as challenging. The governance statement emphasizes the difficulty of balancing adequate departmental budgets with the need to avoid further overspending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has budget discipline. Recent consecutive-year overspends raise questions about financial management capability and control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Overspending confirmed in 2024/25 and 2025/26; 2027/28 flagged as challenging
findings.quote: Setting a balanced budget for 2027/28 will be challenging, particularly given the need to ensure that departmental budgets are adequate to provide the necessary level of services for the people of Gwynedd, and to avoid overspending as seen in 2024/25 and 2025/26.

findings.headline: Audit plan delivery is ahead of quarterly target at 28% completion versus 20% target for Q2
findings.detail: As of 20 September 2026, 11 of 40 audits had been completed with final reports issued, representing 28% completion. The service's quarterly milestone for end of Q2 (second quarter) was 20%. This indicates the Internal Audit function is delivering work ahead of schedule and remains on track to meet the 95% completion target by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Effective delivery of audit work provides independent assurance over council governance and risk management. Timely completion of audits ensures leadership and external stakeholders receive timely oversight information.
findings.figures: 11 audits completed (28% of 40) versus 20% Q2 target; full-year target 95% by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Internal Audit's actual achievement up to 20 September 2026 was 28% - out of 40 individual audits contained in the amended 2026/27 plan, 11 had been released in a finalised version/completed or closed

findings.headline: Follow-up audits on Learning Disability Centres and Residential Homes were cancelled mid-year
findings.detail: The Learning Disability Centres Follow-up (originally 12 days) and Residential Homes Follow-up (originally 7 days) were cancelled in the plan amendments of September 2026. Follow-up audits verify whether management has acted on previous audit findings. Cancelling these means the council will not currently verify that control issues identified in prior audits of these services have been remediated.
findings.matters: Cancelled follow-ups leave previous audit findings unverified for resolution. This creates particular concern given concurrent Limited assurance findings in other adult services, suggesting potential systemic control gaps in the directorate without oversight.
findings.figures: 2 follow-up audits cancelled; 19 days of planned follow-up work removed from plan
findings.quote: Learning Disability Centres Follow-up 12 0 0.0 0.0 Cancelled

findings.headline: Three audits of adult services received Limited assurance ratings, indicating significant control weaknesses
findings.detail: Audits of Cefn Rodyn, Hafod Mawddach, and Direct Payments in the Adults, Health and Wellbeing directorate all completed with Limited assurance ratings. Limited assurance indicates the auditor found material weaknesses in control design or operation. These are the only three Limited ratings among audits with final reports in the 40-audit plan.
findings.matters: Adult services involve vulnerable people and substantial council spending. Control weaknesses in this area indicate governance gaps that could lead to service failures or misuse of funds, creating credit risk.
findings.figures: 3 Limited assurance findings out of 40 total audits; all three in the same directorate
findings.quote: Cefn Rodyn 12 12 9.5 2.5 Final Report Limited

findings.headline: New CIPFA asset indexation requirement for 2025-26 resulted in multiple valuation errors including omitted assets and unsuitable indices
findings.detail: The asset indexation process was introduced as a new CIPFA requirement for 2025-26. Implementation failures included assets being omitted from the indexation process, unsuitable indices applied to certain assets, and some assets excluded from the revaluation process. Errors totaled £0.385m, exceeding the trivial threshold, and the process will be reviewed and corrected for 2026-27 accounts.
findings.matters: Difficulties implementing new financial reporting requirements indicate gaps in financial management processes and technical accounting capability that could affect future financial reporting quality and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: £0.385m in indexation-related errors; described as exceeding the trivial threshold
findings.quote: This process was a new requirement from CIPFA for the 2025/26 accounts and the indexation process will be reviewed and the status of these buildings will be addressed for the 2026 -27 accounts.

findings.headline: Four categories of asset accounting error totaling £4.2m identified in audit but not corrected in 2025-26
findings.detail: Auditors identified uncorrected misstatements in fixed assets: £2.8m from new building work incorrectly categorized as additions to Land and Buildings rather than assets under construction, with demolition costs not recorded as impairment; £0.75m from seven buildings under construction categorized as operational assets; £0.385m from errors in the CIPFA asset indexation process including assets omitted from indexation and unsuitable indices applied; and £0.349m from capital works creditors accrued despite work not being completed. All assessed as immaterial individually and in aggregate; corrections deferred to 2026-27 accounts.
findings.matters: Multiple uncorrected errors in asset values directly affect balance sheet accuracy and reflect control weaknesses in asset accounting processes, a material area affecting council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £2.8m building categorization error; £0.75m construction assets; £0.385m indexation errors; £0.349m accrual error; total £4.283m
findings.quote: The effects of uncorrected misstatements identified during the audit are immaterial, both individually and in the aggregate, to the financial statements taken as a whole.

findings.paper_title: OUTPUT OF THE INTERNAL AUDIT SECTION
findings.headline: Cefn Rodyn residential care home rated Limited assurance with control gaps in care planning, staff training and medication management
findings.detail: Cefn Rodyn, providing residential care for up to 21 residents aged 55+, was rated Limited assurance. Multiple control gaps identified: inadequate monitoring of care plans (risk score 12), staff training gaps in timesheet management (risk score 15), delays in fire testing, non-compliance with mandatory training, gaps in staff medication competency, and inadequate medicine stock control procedures. All risks have agreed management actions.
findings.matters: Multiple control weaknesses in care facility for vulnerable residents; potential impact on resident safety, compliance and council liability
findings.figures: Care home for up to 21 residents aged 55+; six identified risks with scores ranging from 6 to 15
findings.quote: Although controls are in place, compliance with the controls needs to be improved and / or introduces new controls to reduce the risks to which the service is exposed.

findings.paper_title: OUTPUT OF THE INTERNAL AUDIT SECTION
findings.headline: Hafod Mawddach residential care home: Limited assurance and March 2026 pay errors requiring investigation and recovery
findings.detail: Hafod Mawddach, providing residential care for up to 31 residents, received Limited assurance. The audit identified failures in timely reporting of hours worked, resulting in staff receiving incorrect salaries. Specifically, March 2026 pay errors occurred; the agreed action is to investigate these errors and work with the Payroll Service to recover any overpayments.
findings.matters: Actual payroll control failure indicates governance weakness; recovery of overpayments requires council action to resolve the error
findings.figures: Residential facility for up to 31 residents aged 18+

findings.paper_title: OUTPUT OF THE INTERNAL AUDIT SECTION
findings.headline: Direct Payments program worth £2.7m rated Limited assurance with risks around misuse, overpayment and weak oversight
findings.detail: During April 2025 to March 2026, Gwynedd made 1,774 Direct Payments totalling £2.7m to eligible individuals. The audit found Limited assurance, identifying risks that applicants may be unaware of responsibilities, potential for misuse of funds, overpayments accruing, and inadequate accountability for monitoring. New arrangements have been implemented but significant risks remain.
findings.matters: Material sums of public money exposed to inadequate control and monitoring; risk of misuse or overpayment without detection
findings.figures: 1,774 Direct Payments; £2.7 million total
findings.quote: 1774 of Direct Payments were made from the period April 2025 to March 2026. amounting to the equivalent of £2.7million.

findings.headline: No long-term borrowing required based on current capital and revenue projections through to 2029.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark, which calculates the minimum external borrowing needed, projects declining requirements from £24.7m in 2027 to £19.6m in 2029, assuming no new capital funded by borrowing and 50-year straight-line revenue provision for new capital. The council's existing £73.9m borrowing portfolio is sufficient to cover these projections.
findings.matters: Indicates the council has sufficient existing debt to cover medium-term capital and revenue needs without additional borrowing, demonstrating sustainable debt positioning and reducing refinancing pressure.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark: £24.7m (31.3.27), £22.1m (31.3.28), £19.6m (31.3.29); existing borrowing £73.9m
findings.quote: The chart shows that there is no need to borrow long - term based on current projections.

findings.headline: Strong liquidity position with £79.2m available to meet unexpected payments within three months, nearly eight times the operational target.
findings.detail: The council maintains significant cash reserves available within a rolling 3-month period without additional borrowing, measured at £79.2m against a target of £10m. Total investment balances ranged between £61.2m and £128.8m during the quarter due to timing differences between income and expenditure.
findings.matters: Demonstrates robust cash buffer to absorb unexpected demands, market disruption, or revenue shocks without emergency borrowing, strengthening council creditworthiness.

findings.headline: Council undertook no new borrowing in Q1 2026/27 and maintains a conservative internal borrowing strategy to reduce interest costs.
findings.detail: The council pursued a deliberate strategy of keeping borrowing below underlying levels to reduce risk and interest costs. No new borrowing was undertaken in the first quarter, enabling cost reductions despite foregoing investment income. Total borrowing remained unchanged at £73.9m.
findings.matters: Demonstrates disciplined debt management and active cost control, which reassures lenders about the council's approach to affordability.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £73.9m (unchanged from 31 March); net investments £11.4m
findings.quote: No new borrowing was undertaken in the first quarter of 2026/27. This strategy enabled the Council to reduce net borrowing costs (despite foregoing investment income) and reduce overall treasury risk.

findings.headline: LGPS pension reserve corrected for £10.656m discrepancy; pension fund settled to £nil on cessation
findings.detail: On 31 May 2025 when GwE ceased operations, its LGPS pension fund was settled to a £nil closing balance. Audit identified a £10.656m discrepancy between the opening pension reserve in the actuarial report and the financial statements, caused by an omitted asset ceiling adjustment. The actuary revised the report and consequential pension entries and disclosures were corrected throughout the financial statements.
findings.matters: Pension settlements represent closure of major balance sheet liabilities; a £10.656m correction demonstrates the importance of rigorous audit review in complex organizational transitions involving pension scheme settlements.
findings.figures: £10.656m discrepancy; £nil closing pension balance
findings.quote: A £10.656m discrepancy was identified between the opening pension reserve in the IAS 19 actuarial report and the financial statements due to omission of an asset ceiling adjustment. The opening balance was confirmed as correct. The IAS 19 actuarial report was revised to reflect the correct position.

findings.headline: Education grant funding now flows directly to councils, making each council solely responsible for grant compliance and terms.
findings.detail: Welsh Government centralized pre-16 education grants into the Local Authority Education Grant (LAEG) from 2024-25. Councils now receive funding directly rather than through GwE, and hold sole responsibility for managing grant compliance and terms and conditions. This shifts financial and regulatory risk from the regional consortium to individual councils.
findings.matters: Gwynedd now carries sole responsibility for LAEG compliance and its terms and conditions, which is a material change in risk and regulatory obligation compared to the previous shared responsibility model.
findings.figures: 2024-25 onwards
findings.quote: Following the Welsh Government decision to amalgamate the main education grants under one heading, the Local Authority Education Grant (LAEG) from 2024-25 onwards, the grant has been paid to the Local Authorities to manage and delegate funding directly to schools. The requirements, risks, terms and conditions of the grant are now the sole responsibility of the individual Local Authorities.

findings.headline: GwE changed from a regional joint service to a commissioned service under Welsh Government's education restructuring.
findings.detail: In response to Welsh Government's December 2023 decision to centralize education grants, GwE's operational model shifted fundamentally. Rather than being a joint regional service, it now provides commissioned services to councils. Strategic direction for school improvement is now provided by Chief Education Officers, not GwE leadership. This represents a significant change in governance and accountability structures.
findings.matters: This restructuring redistributes risk and accountability: Gwynedd, as host authority, now manages education funding and grant compliance for a service it funds but no longer directly controls, requiring careful attention to financial and governance risks.
findings.figures: 6 councils; December 2023
findings.quote: GwE has changed from being a 'regional joint service' to a commissioned service.

findings.headline: Six North Wales councils reduced their funding contributions to GwE's core service by 10% in 2024-25.
findings.detail: All six councils that partner in GwE made a deliberate decision to reduce their core funding contribution by 10% for the 2024-25 financial year. This follows Welsh Government's restructuring of education grants and represents a significant cost reduction for a regional service on which all councils depend.
findings.matters: A coordinated 10% funding cut from six partner councils signals budget pressure across the region; a council finance director must understand the sustainability of partner-funded services at reduced levels.
findings.quote: The GwE Budget for 2024-25 also reflects a decision by the six Local Authorities to reduce their contribution to the core service by 10%.

findings.headline: GwE's final accounts received an unqualified audit opinion
findings.detail: Audit Wales has provided an unqualified opinion on the Statement of Accounts for 2025/26, the final accounts for the joint committee following closure on 31 May 2025. The audit identified issues outlined in Appendix 2 of the ISA260 report, but these were not material enough to affect the opinion.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion confirms Gwynedd properly managed and reported the financial wind-down of the joint venture, indicating sound financial stewardship and governance controls.
findings.quote: Page 5 of the report states an "unqualified opinion on the accounts" for 2025/26.

findings.headline: New CIPFA indexation process requirements for 2025-26 generated multiple errors, with controls not yet embedded
findings.detail: CIPFA introduced new asset indexation requirements in 2025-26. Multiple individual errors were identified in their application: assets omitted from indexation process, incorrect indices applied to some assets, assets incorrectly excluded from revaluation, and required desktop valuations not undertaken. Auditor recommends enhanced review and quality assurance between finance team and valuer.
findings.matters: Property assets form a material part of council balance sheets; a new measurement process has generated multiple errors in year one of implementation, indicating that controls over this material process are not yet effective.
findings.figures: £0.385m identified in aggregate as exceeding triviality threshold; multiple process failures identified across indexation and valuation
findings.quote: A number of individually trivial issues were identified in relation to the application of the new asset indexation requirements. Whilst we recognise that supporting guidance from CIPFA was issued later in the financial year and this was the first year of implementation, these findings highlight opportunities to strengthen review and quality assurance arrangements between the finance team and valuer.

findings.headline: Material corrected errors totalling over £18 million indicate initial accounting treatments for significant transactions were incorrect
findings.detail: During audit, management corrected: £14.5m net book value of a school building incorrectly classified as a Right of Use Asset (should be land and buildings); £1.941m where capitalised costs were incorrectly credited to income rather than offset against expenditure; and £1.424m of investment income misclassified as service income. All were corrected before accounts sign-off but indicate initial transaction accounting did not capture substance of arrangements.
findings.matters: While corrections were made, the scale and nature of errors (£18m+ in adjustments) indicates that first-line controls and initial accounting review processes did not prevent material misstatements in complex transactions, particularly around capital and lease accounting.
findings.figures: £14.540m, £1.941m, £1.424m (totalling over £18m of corrections needed)
findings.quote: Audit testing identified that a school building constructed and funded by the Council on leased land had been incorrectly classified and transferred as a Right of Use Asset. As only the land lease falls within the scope of IFRS 16, the building should have remained classified as Land and Buildings to reflect the substance of the arrangement and comply with the CIPFA Code of Practice.

findings.headline: Approximately £3.9 million in uncorrected property, plant and equipment misstatements remain in the accounts
findings.detail: Council has not corrected multiple accounting errors in property assets: £2.8m overstatement of land and buildings in a building redevelopment (includes £0.3m unrecorded impairment of demolished building); £0.75m of assets misclassified as operational when still under construction; £0.385m in aggregate valuation and indexation errors; and £0.349m in capital work accrued at year-end when work was incomplete. Management has classified all as immaterial.
findings.matters: A pattern of property accounting weaknesses in material amounts indicates potential control deficiencies in a key balance sheet area; uncorrected errors of this scale suggest either weak initial controls or a materiality judgment that a lender should understand.
findings.figures: £2.829m, £0.750m, £0.385m, £0.349m (totalling approximately £3.9m); property, plant and equipment is typically a council's largest balance sheet category
findings.quote: Expenditure of £2.511 million incurred during the year on the redevelopment of an asset was incorrectly classified as additions to Land and Buildings rather than Assets Under Construction. As the new facility was not operational as at 31 March 2026, the expenditure should have been classified as an addition to Asset Under Construction. In addition, the original building, which was demolished as part of the redevelopment, had not been impaired, resulting in an overstatement of Land and Building of £0.318 million.

findings.headline: Material errors in related party disclosures identified for third consecutive year, indicating control environment weakness
findings.detail: Despite introduction of a dedicated working paper to address prior-year issues, material errors were again identified in related party member and officer disclosures in 2025-26. The working paper was not completed or reviewed effectively, and the cumulative impact of corrections totalled £16.659 million. Auditor concludes that existing quality review arrangements are not operating effectively in this area.
findings.matters: Related party transactions are material by nature and high-interest to lenders and regulators; a control failure recurring for three consecutive years suggests the finance function's review processes are not effective and raises questions about internal oversight of material disclosures.
findings.figures: £16.659 million cumulative impact of corrections; errors identified for third consecutive year
findings.quote: This is the third consecutive year in which audit testing has identified material errors within the related party disclosures. Although a dedicated working paper was introduced to address issues identified in the previous years, it was not completed or reviewed effectively during 2025-26, resulting in material misstatements within the disclosures. The recurring nature of these errors indicates that existing quality review arrangements are not operating effectively in this area.

findings.headline: Audit costs exceeded £34,832 estimate due to complexity of first full accounts after April 2025 NWEAB transfer; final fee not yet agreed.
findings.detail: This was the first year the NWCJC prepared a full set of financial statements following the transfer of NWEAB arrangements on 1 April 2025. The audit required more work than originally anticipated to understand new governance arrangements, reporting requirements, accounting treatments, and opening balances transferred from the previous body. The auditors note audit complexity increased the level of input required beyond the original estimate, and will discuss additional costs with the Statutory Finance Officer before agreeing the final fee.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils undergoing similar organizational transitions need to understand the audit and compliance costs associated with major restructurings; overruns indicate the level of effort required to establish new accounting systems, governance frameworks, and transition procedures.
findings.figures: Original estimate: £34,832; final fee to be agreed
findings.quote: As this was the first year that the North Wales CJC prepared a full set of financial statements following the transfer of the North Wales Economic Ambition Board arrangements on 1 April 2025, the audit involved more work than originally anticipated.

findings.headline: Welsh Government Parc Bryn Cegin joint arrangement accounting treatment remained unconfirmed; classified as Joint Operation pending government clarification.
findings.detail: The NWCJC entered a new collaborative arrangement with Welsh Government for a project development where Welsh Government provides land and the NWCJC provides funding. The auditors assessed and concluded the arrangement should be classified as a Joint Operation rather than a Joint Venture, but clarification sought from Welsh Government on accounting treatment had not been received before audit completion. Auditors were therefore unable to fully conclude on whether the treatment adopted is appropriate. Any potential impact is not expected to be material to 2025-26 but requires monitoring as the arrangement develops.
findings.matters: Collaborative arrangements with government can significantly affect the recognition of assets and liabilities; uncertainty about accounting treatment creates risk that future financial statements may require adjustment as the arrangement develops, affecting lender assessments of net asset positions.
findings.figures: Parc Bryn Cegin project (amount not disclosed in audit report)
findings.quote: During the audit, we identified uncertainty regarding the accounting treatment of the collaborative agreement with Welsh Government for Parc Bryn Cegin

findings.headline: £6.9 million loan advanced during 2025-26 required cash flow statement reclassification; £1.9 million undrawn balance also identified.
findings.detail: The NWCJC advanced a loan of £6,942,000 during 2025-26, which was correctly recognized as a debtor on the balance sheet. The related cash outflow was initially misclassified in the cash flow statement as an investing activity but was corrected to show consistent accounting treatment. A further £1,923,000 undrawn element of the loan facility was identified and added to the financial instruments disclosure.
findings.matters: A £6.9 million loan transaction represents material new financing activity that affects cash flows and asset composition. The initial misclassification indicates the organization was establishing new types of financial arrangements that may require enhanced financial controls and management systems.
findings.figures: £6,942,000 loan advanced; £1,923,000 undrawn balance
findings.quote: A loan advanced during the year was correctly recognised as a debtor in the Balance Sheet; however, the related cash outflow had been incorrectly classified as an investing activity within the Cash Flow Statement.

findings.detail: The CJC is in receipt of a 3-year Welsh Government grant funding agreement to support transformation and capacity building. All known funding is included in the Medium Term Financial Plan. The organization will face the conclusion of this dedicated funding stream within the planning period.
findings.matters: Reliance on time-limited grant funding creates financial uncertainty when the agreement concludes; stakeholders need clarity on how the organization will sustain the capabilities and services established with grant funding once that support ends.

findings.detail: The report states that budget constraints are being 'managed carefully' and that affordability is being 'aligned to prioritisation of projects within the programme'. The Statutory Finance Officer notes that capacity is 'under constant review due to the nature of the transformation project' and that additional funding, if required, would be sought from underspends in other budget headings.
findings.matters: A newly established public body managing a transformation programme within constrained budgets indicates execution risk; reliance on reallocating underspends from elsewhere to fund additional needs could affect other services or require further scope reduction.

findings.headline: North Wales Growth Deal 2026/27 budget of £3.15m funded by six councils, four educational institutions, and three government grant streams
findings.detail: The Growth Deal budget of £3,148,240 is funded by contributions from six local authorities (Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Anglesey, Wrexham: £58,730 each), four educational institutions (Bangor University, Wrexham University, Coleg Cambria, Grŵp Llandrillo Menai: £29,380 each), plus supplementary local authority contributions (£40,000 each), North Wales Growth Deal grants totalling £1,095,350, Welsh Government energy grant £176,000, UK Shared Prosperity Fund £26,170, and reserves £986,730.

This represents a restructuring of permanent base-funded roles into project-specific positions.
findings.matters: Shifts from base staffing to project-only staffing affect organizational capacity for sustained operations; councils co-funding the CJC need to understand whether this represents planned evolution or reflects constraints on permanent headcount.

These combined drawdowns total £1,611,320 against three budgets, representing 53% of the strategic services net expenditure and 31% of the Growth Deal budget. Both drawdowns appear in base budgets as planned contributions, not in-year adjustments.
findings.matters: Large reserve drawdowns indicate the extent to which these multi-partner organizations rely on accumulated funds rather than current-year revenue; councils co-funding these bodies and lenders assess financial sustainability and the pace at which reserves are being depleted.

findings.detail: The Growth Deal is forecasted to underspend by £288,174 against budget, primarily from employee costs. Around £348,000 of the underspend reflects staff now funded by Ambition North Wales Growth Deal projects (£16,000 also relating to CJC time and £38,000 to Regional Skills Partnership). findings.headline: Investment Zone achieving neutral 2026/27 position through use of interest on grant balances (£227,589), with this arrangement flagged as temporary and unsustainable
findings.detail: The Investment Zone has £200,000 annual grant allocation. To achieve a neutral 2026/27 position, the CJC is using interest earned on Investment Zone grant balances of £227,589 to supplement this allocation. The report explicitly identifies this as temporary, noting that the arrangement will not be viable from 2027/28 onwards as cash outflows from distributing the grant will reduce the balance earning interest.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer authorities need to understand whether Investment Zone operating costs are sustainable within core funding; using interest as gap-funding indicates annual grant allocation may be insufficient for ongoing administration, requiring either higher contributions from councils or reduced scope in future years.
findings.figures: Interest on Investment Zone balances used: £227,589; annual grant allocation: £200,000
findings.quote: In order to leave a neutral position for the Investment Zone, interest from the Investment Zone grant balances of £227,589 will be used, in addition to the £200,000 grant allocation. The use of interest is a temporary arrangement as the cash outflows from distributing the Investment Zone grant will reduce the interest income.

findings.headline: Growth Deal capital programme slippage of £15.81m (23.6% of budget) in 2026/27 forecast, attributed to project delays and partially offset by Business Gateway project introduction
findings.detail: The Growth Deal capital programme approved budget of £67.07m for 2026/27 is now forecast to deliver expenditure of £51.26m, a reduction of £15.81m. This is attributed to slippage on existing projects. Introduction of the Business Gateway project and brought-forward expenditure on Reserve List projects have reduced (but not eliminated) the slippage.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer authorities assess capital delivery performance as an indicator of project management capacity and spending efficiency; a 23.6% variance in a single year requires understanding whether this is a timing issue or reflects systemic delivery constraints or over-optimistic planning.
findings.figures: Approved budget: £67.07m; estimated expenditure: £51.26m; slippage: £15.81m
findings.quote: There is a net reduction of £15.81m in the anticipated expenditure for 2026/27 and this is due to slippage on projects. However, the introduction of the Business Gateway project in the capital profile and the brought forward expenditure on the Reserve List projects have reduced the slippage.

findings.headline: CJC reserves forecast to fall from £1,636,007 to £971,543 with additional draw of £39,874 beyond planned allocation, and further draws expected in future years
findings.detail: The CJC reserve opened at £1,636,007 at 31 March 2026. The 2026/27 budget planned to allocate £624,590 from reserves. The July review forecasts an additional £39,874 draw to achieve a neutral position, reducing reserves to £971,543. The report explicitly states this pattern is expected to continue: resourcing requirements are increasing and the discretionary CJC implementation grant is neither expected nor confirmed for future years, implying further reserve draws are anticipated.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer authorities assess reserve sustainability as a measure of financial resilience; a newly formed joint committee drawing reserves at this rate (£664,464 in year one) without confirmed replacement grants faces reserve depletion within two years if the pattern continues, which would require council support or spending reductions.
findings.figures: Reserve at 31 March 2026: £1,636,007; allocated to budget: £624,590; additional forecast draw: £39,874; forecast balance at 31 March 2027: £971,543
findings.quote: In order to leave a neutral position for 2026/27, a transfer of an additional £39,874 is required from the reserve, therefore the estimated balance at 31 March 2027 is £971,543. It is expected that this will be required for future budgets, with the CJC resourcing requirements increasing and grants such as the CJC implementation grant not expected or confirmed.

findings.headline: CJC legal services overspend of £105,945 against budgeted support of £130,280, driven by interim Monitoring Officer and Deputy Monitoring Officer appointments
findings.detail: The CJC budgeted £130,280 for legal support across Additional Monitoring Officer Capacity, Support Services, and Set-up costs headings, based on partial FTE allocations. Actual engagement of an interim Monitoring Officer at full-time cost, plus interim Deputy Monitoring Officer, plus contracted legal support has produced forecast expenditure of £236,225. The budget assumed 0.35 FTE Monitoring Officer and 0.18 FTE Section 151 Officer from support services; actual arrangement is full-time interim Monitoring Officer with supporting interim Deputy.

findings.detail: The 10-year Investment Zone programme provides £6.4m total administration funding. findings.matters: An administration funding allocation insufficient for stated costs in year one signals either scope creep in the programme's administrative needs or an underfunded budget design for a ten-year scheme.

findings.headline: Statutory Strategic Development Plan duty assigned with no identified grant funding, creating unfunded cost pressure on levy
findings.detail: The CJC has a statutory duty under the Local Government and Elections (Wales) Act 2021 to produce a Strategic Development Plan. A September 2025 report found there is no identified funding from Welsh Government for the SDP, in contrast to the published commitment to support Regional Transport Plan work. The organization must meet the full SDP costs from levy funding. Expenditure is forecast at £814,210 (2027/28), £634,690 (2028/29) and £625,910 (2029/30), declining as external consultants are replaced by in-house resources.
findings.matters: A statutory duty assigned without corresponding funding creates a permanent cost pressure on the organization's general levy and demonstrates the risk of unfunded mandates on regional bodies.
findings.quote: A report to the Strategic Planning Sub-Committee on 4th September 2025 highlighted that the Regulations relating to developing the SDP clearly set out that the production of an SDP is a statutory duty for the CJC, and implicit with that is the responsibility to meet the full costs of doing so. Apart from some early modest start-up grant funding, there is no identified funding for the SDP from Welsh Government, unlike a published commitment to support Regional Transport Plan work. As things stand, it is therefore up to the CJC to meet the full costs of the SDP.

findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to fall from £839,851 to zero by end of plan period, leaving only minimum 5% general reserve
findings.detail: Reserves at 31 March 2026 were £1,636,007. After approved and estimated usage in 2026/27 of £664,464, reserves at 31 March 2027 will be £971,543. The general reserve minimum is set at 5% of gross revenue budget (£131,692), leaving £839,851 available for use. The MTFP forecasts all available earmarked reserves will be exhausted by 31 March 2030, leaving only the £131,692 minimum. The organization had previously acknowledged holding more reserves than necessary.
findings.matters: Forecast depletion of discretionary reserves removes the organization's financial resilience to handle unexpected cost pressures or opportunities, and removes any buffer to dampen future levy increases.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap of £2.1-2.2m annually forces choice between unaffordable levy increases (30-113%) or near-complete depletion of reserves by 2030
findings.detail: The CJC faces annual deficits of £2,163,830 (2027/28), £2,123,000 (2028/29) and £2,212,080 (2029/30) to be funded by constituent authority levies and reserves. Four funding options are presented: freezing the levy is unfeasible (would need £1,148,650 of reserves the CJC does not have); increasing levy 113% is deemed unjustifiable; a 71% increase with 50% annual reserve drawdown would leave reserves depleted by 2030; a 30% increase would exhaust all available reserves in 2027/28, requiring 60%+ increases in subsequent years.
findings.matters: A multi-year structural gap between expenditure and sustainable funding signals either the organization is undertaking unfunded statutory duties or has insufficient constituent council commitment to fund its remit, creating financial instability.

findings.quote: Whilst there are clear opportunities arising from the increase in the statutory duties on Ambition North Wales to improve regional working and attract significant investment into the region, there remains the challenge of securing funding.

findings.headline: Projected borrowing requirement in 2027/28 on Growth Deal due to timing mismatch between capital expenditure and grant funding profile
findings.detail: The CJC forecasts a medium-term temporary funding gap between Growth Deal capital expenditure and government grant funding. Welsh Government has not yet confirmed its revised grant profile for £16m of funding withheld in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Government grant payments are also delayed, received at year-end or slipping into the following financial year. As a result, the CJC is forecasting it will need to borrow to fund capital expenditure in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A council borrowing due to grant timing mismatches rather than capital investment creates a cash-flow refinancing risk and means the lender is funding a working capital gap, not productive assets.
findings.figures: Growth Deal funding withheld: £16m (status: Welsh Government not yet confirmed in revised grant profile); Projected need to borrow: 2027/28
findings.quote: We are currently forecasting that in 2027/28, the CJC will need to borrow to fund the capital expenditure. findings.detail: The Head of Finance has stated explicitly that there is a significant risk of severe financial instability if the CJC does not take early and decisive action to address its funding position. This statement is made in the context of explaining why both reserve depletion and massive levy increases appear unavoidable.
findings.matters: An explicit financial instability warning from a statutory finance officer is a material governance red flag indicating systemic financial problems requiring urgent remedial action and close external monitoring.

Options show a choice between immediate steep increases or phased increases with eventual reserve exhaustion.
findings.matters: Levy increases of this magnitude represent substantial cost increases to constituent councils; finance directors need to understand the CJC's options and the trade-offs between immediate and deferred funding gaps.

findings.matters: Reserve depletion and inability to maintain service funding at prior levels signal financial stress; councils facing similar pressures need to understand how peers manage reserve limitations and what constraints they face.

findings.headline: CJC levy apportionment to constituent councils must be agreed unanimously each year.
findings.detail: Regulations require that the CJC's apportionment to the six constituent councils and Eryri National Park Authority must be agreed unanimously by all levying bodies. Combined with the absence of long-term Welsh Government funding, this creates an annual funding negotiation with no automatic continuation and no default mechanism if agreement cannot be reached.
findings.matters: A decision-making structure requiring unanimous consent from all funding bodies, with no long-term funding guarantee and a statutory deadline of 31 January, creates operational risk if any council withholds agreement to fund CJC statutory functions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: CJC's non-grant-funded statutory functions have no long-term sustainable funding mechanism from Welsh Government.
findings.detail: Apart from the Growth Deal (funded by UK and Welsh Government grants with a 2.15% top-slice) and Investment Zones (grant-funded), the CJC must fund its strategic planning, transport and economic wellbeing functions through annual levies on constituent councils. findings.matters: Rising casework backlogs in a specific area can indicate either process bottlenecks or workload changes. Peer finance officers monitor whether colleagues are managing pension administration workload within capacity.
