findings.quote: Although the team completed 1,167 cases, 1,635 new cases were received during the year, resulting in the backlog increasing from 1,304 to 1,772. This was the only area where a significant increase in outstanding cases was recorded.

findings.headline: 2025 actuarial valuation confirmed strong funding level, prompting investment strategy review.
findings.detail: The triennial actuarial valuation in 2025 found the Fund adequately funded. In response, the Committee reviewed and reset investment strategy in November 2025, moving to reduce equity allocation and shift toward income-generating assets including natural capital. This represents a planned de-risking strategy enabled by the strong funding position rather than corrective action.
findings.matters: A strong funding level means the council's future pension contributions should remain manageable without unexpected increases. The strategy shift demonstrates active management of liability as the fund matures.
findings.figures: 2025 actuarial valuation conducted; investment strategy reviewed November 2025
findings.quote: The 2025 actuarial valuation demonstrated once a gain that the Fund has a strong funding level and therefore a review of the investment strategy was undertaken in November 2025. The review confirmed that the Fund should continue to de-risk by reducing its equity allocation and invest in income generating assets

findings.headline: Pension fund value increased to £3.6 billion with 10.9% returns against 11.5% benchmark.
findings.detail: The Gwynedd Pension Fund grew from £3.2 billion to £3.6 billion during 2025-26. The Fund returned 10.9% for the year against its benchmark of 11.5%. The average LGPS fund delivered 9.6% for the year, meaning Gwynedd exceeded peer average performance. Strong investment returns reduce the funding pressure on the council as employer.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's pension scheme is adequately funded and its asset base growing. Strong returns and a rising fund value reduce the employer contribution burden on the council's budget.
findings.figures: Fund value £3.2 billion (2025) to £3.6 billion (2026); fund return 10.9% vs benchmark 11.5% vs LGPS average 9.6%
findings.quote: the value of the Pension Fund increased from £3.2 billion to £3.6 billion. The Fund saw positive returns of 10.9% over the year, against a benchmark of 11.5%. The average LGPS fund delivered a return of 9.6% for the year

findings.headline: McCloud remedy project on track for completion with majority of work finished
findings.detail: The McCloud remedy project remains on track. The majority of work required to implement the remedy has been completed. Current efforts focus on resolving the remaining transfer cases affected by the regulations — the final significant element of the project. Once these cases are completed, remaining McCloud-related activities will form part of normal business-as-usual administration.
findings.matters: Major regulatory compliance project on track; completion reduces ongoing regulatory risk and frees resources from project to routine administration.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The team remains on track to complete the remaining project work in line with agreed timescales.

findings.headline: New iTrent payroll system implementation scheduled for early 2027, with testing from autumn 2026
findings.detail: Cyngor Gwynedd is implementing a new iTrent payroll system with Pension Fund participation in design and development. System testing is planned for autumn 2026, with implementation in early 2027. The system is expected to deliver reduced manual data input, automated processing of payroll activities, fewer manual reconciliations, improved accuracy and efficiency, and reduced operational risk.
findings.matters: Represents a capital investment project important to pension administration, which depends on accurate payroll data.
findings.figures: Autumn 2026, early 2027
findings.quote: Current plans are for system testing to commence during Autumn 2026, with implementation anticipated in early 2027.

findings.headline: Legal & General appointed as AVC provider from 1 September 2026, following challenges with Clerical Medical
findings.detail: Following a comprehensive review by Hymans Robertson, the Fund switched Additional Voluntary Contributions providers from Clerical Medical to Legal & General from 1 September 2026. The review identified operational and administrative challenges experienced over the previous two years with the Clerical Medical arrangement. The new provider offers lower member charges, wider investment choices, and improved online member portal functionality.
findings.matters: Indicates the fund previously experienced operational problems; the provider change should improve efficiency and member experience.
findings.figures: 1 September 2026, past two years
findings.quote: The review identified a number of challenges relating to the Fund's previous arrangements with Clerical Medical, particularly in relation to administrative and operational processes experienced over the past two years.

findings.headline: Additional administrative workload expected, met by appointing Apprentice and Trainee Pension Officer on 20 July 2026
findings.detail: The Fund's regulatory changes and retrospective benefit work are creating additional administrative workload. In response, an Apprentice and Trainee Pension Officer joined the team on 20 July 2026. The appointments explicitly support succession planning and resilience 'as workloads continue to increase'. Additional administrative workload is expected to continue over the coming months as retrospective cases are reviewed and regulatory implications emerge.
findings.matters: Indicates increasing operational complexity and ongoing cost pressures in pension administration as workloads are expected to continue rising.
findings.figures: 20 July 2026
findings.quote: The additional resource will support succession planning, strengthen the resilience of the team and assist with maintaining high levels of service delivery as workloads continue to increase.

findings.headline: Fit for the Future reforms mandate appointment of Senior LGPS Officer by 31 December 2026
findings.detail: Regulatory reforms in force from June 2026 require LGPS administering authorities to appoint a designated Senior LGPS Officer with overall responsibility for fund management and governance, and to appoint an independent committee member and adopt an Administration Strategy Statement. These must be implemented by end of 2026. Officers are assessing implications and will report further to ensure compliance within the prescribed timescales.
findings.matters: Requires investment in a new senior management role and represents a regulatory compliance deadline by end of 2026.
findings.figures: 31 December 2026
findings.quote: administering authorities are expected to implement the key governance requirements, including the appointment of a Senior LGPS Officer, the appointment of an independent committee member, and adoption of an Administration Strategy Statement, by 31 December 2026.

findings.headline: Access and Fairness reforms introduce retrospective pension benefit changes from 1 April 2014
findings.detail: The LGPS reforms implemented from 1 April 2026 include retrospective elements affecting survivor benefits and death grants. Critically, removal of the age 75 restriction on death grants applies retrospectively to qualifying deaths from 1 April 2014 — a decade back. The Fund must identify affected beneficiaries, a process complicated by the need to trace individuals who may have died or relocated since the original member's death.
findings.matters: Increases pension fund liabilities which the council must fund, affecting its balance sheet and cash requirements.
findings.figures: 1 April 2014
findings.quote: Removal of the age 75 restriction on death grants, extending eligibility and applying the change retrospectively to qualifying deaths from 1 April 2014.

findings.headline: WPP IM Co received 'Minded to Approve' letter from FCA
findings.detail: The Wales Pension Partnership's investment management company, established in August 2025 with Rob Lamb appointed CEO in September 2025, has received a 'Minded to Approve' letter from the FCA. This represents regulatory progress on the investment management operation serving the pension fund.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to track regulatory compliance and approvals affecting the pension fund's investment management structure and operational framework.
findings.figures: WPP IM Co established August 2025; CEO appointed September 2025
findings.quote: Confirmation that the WPP IM Co had received the 'Minded to Approve' letter from the FCA

findings.headline: Interest income of £1.7m exceeded budget of £1.6m despite falling interest rates
findings.detail: The council received £1.7m in interest on deposits in 2025-26, outperforming the budgeted £1.6m by £0.1m. This occurred despite bank rate falling from 4.50% in May 2025 to 3.75% by December 2025, and the council's portfolio average return declining from 4.82% to 4.49%.
findings.matters: Interest income outperformance provides additional non-tax revenue in year, though falling interest rates will require lower budget assumptions going forward
findings.figures: Actual interest £1.7m, budget £1.6m, variance £0.1m; portfolio rate fell from 4.82% to 4.49%; bank rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75%
findings.quote: total interest received on deposits was £1.7m which was higher than the budgeted level of £1.6m

findings.headline: Investment balances fell by £56.9m to £96.0m, a 37% reduction, with no stated cause
findings.detail: The council's treasury investment portfolio declined from £152.9m at 31 March 2025 to £96.0m at 31 March 2026. The paper records the movement across each asset class but provides no explanation for this substantial drawdown. Balances ranged between £73.5m and £159.8m during the year.
findings.matters: A significant unexplained reduction in investment balances signals either planned revenue/capital spending, working capital usage, or changed cash position with implications for future liquidity and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: Opening balance £152.9m, closing balance £96.0m, reduction £56.9m; intra-year range £73.5m to £159.8m
findings.quote: During the year, the Council's investment balances have ranged between £73.5 million and £159.8 million.

findings.headline: Council exceeded approved investment limits for unsecured banks and money market funds during 2025-26
findings.detail: The council held maximum amounts during the year of £5m in unsecured bank deposits (against an approved limit of £4m) and £10m in money market funds (against a limit of £8m). The section 151 officer identified that this resulted from following historical limits rather than updated guidance. Measures have been implemented to prevent recurrence.
findings.matters: Breaches of investment policy limits indicate control process failures and could reflect broader governance weaknesses affecting financial management and creditworthiness
findings.figures: Unsecured banks: £5m maximum against £4m limit; Money market funds: £10m maximum against £8m limit
findings.quote: The limits imposed on two occasions were not fully complied with because historical limits had been followed. Measures are now in place to update the guidance immediately.

findings.headline: Bail-in exposure on deposits increased from 50% to 58%, concentrating counterparty risk
findings.detail: The proportion of the Council's investments held in institutions subject to deposit bail-in (potential clawback if banks fail) increased from 50% at March 2025 to 58% at March 2026. While still below the average for all local authorities (64%), the upward trend means an increasing share of the investment portfolio would be at risk of loss if a counterparty fails.
findings.matters: Higher bail-in exposure means larger potential loss if any deposit counterparty fails; the trend indicates the council is drifting toward greater concentration of counterparty risk
findings.figures: Bail-in exposure: 50% at 31.03.2025, 58% at 31.03.2026; All LAs average 64%

findings.headline: £12.2m held in strategic pooled equity and property funds with no defined maturity; 5.74% return used to fund current-year services
findings.detail: The Council holds £12.2m in externally managed strategic pooled funds (equity, bonds, property) with no defined maturity date, explicitly stating these funds are used to 'support services in year'. These funds generated 5.74% income return plus £0.3m unrealised capital gain in 2025-26. However, the document acknowledges capital values move both 'up and down on months, quarters and even years', creating potential revenue volatility if markets decline.
findings.matters: Relying on pooled fund returns to fund annual service delivery creates vulnerability: if markets decline, capital values fall and the council may either need to draw more than planned or find alternative funding, creating a hidden revenue risk
findings.figures: £12.2m invested in strategic pooled funds; 5.74% income return used for services; £0.3m unrealised capital gain in 2025-26
findings.quote: These funds generated an income return of 5.74% which is used to support services in year, and an unrealised capital gain of £0.3m in this financial year. Because these funds have no defined maturity date, but are available for withdrawal after a notice period... capital values will move both up and down on months, quarters and even years

findings.headline: Council held £5m in unsecured bank deposits against £4m approved limit; held money market funds at £8m ceiling in 2025-26
findings.detail: The Council breached two investment limits during 2025-26. It held £5m in unsecured bank deposits when the approved limit was £4m, and held money market funds at the £8m ceiling. The section 151 officer states these breaches occurred because staff 'followed historical limits' rather than updated guidance, indicating the finance function's internal control procedures were not sufficiently tight to catch the change.
findings.matters: Control failures on investment limits suggest the finance function's compliance procedures lack adequate monitoring; this raises questions about the effectiveness of internal controls more broadly
findings.figures: Unsecured banks: £5m actual held against £4m limit; Money Market Funds: £8m actual against £8m limit; two non-compliances flagged
findings.quote: The limits imposed on two occasions were not fully complied with because historical limits had been followed. Measures are now in place to update the guidance immediately.

findings.headline: Council's engagement and consultation capability escalated to high-risk during 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's own governance risk assessment identified that its ability to engage effectively with service users has deteriorated, moving from medium to high risk. The council explicitly states that "the preparation and conduct of consultations and engagement exercises remains very challenging" despite efforts. Resolution is planned but deferred: a review of engagement processes is scheduled for 2026/27, with a revised strategy to follow in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender needs to know whether a council can effectively consult on service changes and budget decisions, as engagement failure directly affects the council's ability to manage change, set balanced budgets, and maintain stakeholder confidence through difficult financial periods.
findings.figures: Risk score increased from 9 (medium) to 12 (high) during 2025/26
findings.quote: Despite all efforts, the preparation and conduct of consultations and engagement exercises remains very challenging. In 2026/27 we will address this by undertaking a review of the Council's engagement processes before moving on to the formulation and presentation of a revised Engagement Strategy in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: HEAD OF INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT 2025/2026
findings.headline: Control weaknesses identified in prior years persist unresolved in follow-up audits
findings.detail: Follow-up reviews of audits from 2024/25 that received Limited assurance show several areas remain at Limited assurance, including Breakfast Clubs, School Transportation, Homelessness Prevention Grant, and others. This indicates that management actions intended to remedy control weaknesses have not been effective.
findings.matters: Persistent control weaknesses across multiple years suggest management is not effectively implementing corrective actions. This indicates either a systemic inability or unwillingness to improve, reducing confidence in management's financial discipline.
findings.figures: Multiple 2024/25 Limited assurance audits followed up in 2025/26: Breakfast Clubs Limited, School Transportation Limited, Homelessness Prevention Grant Limited, Plas Pengwaith Limited, Category Management Environment Limited.
findings.quote: Breakfast Clubs Follow Up Final Report Limited 21 May 2026

findings.paper_title: HEAD OF INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT 2025/2026
findings.headline: Audit quality and completion targets significantly missed across all corporate indicators
findings.detail: The audit function underperformed on three core performance measures: audit plan completion fell to 88% versus 95% ambition; only 51.28% of audits achieved Satisfactory or higher assurance versus 80% corporate target; and only 53.57% of high or very high risk agreed actions were implemented within timetable versus 100% target.
findings.matters: Missed audit completion and quality targets mean reduced oversight of council services and finances. High-risk agreed actions not being implemented means identified control risks remain unmitigated.
findings.figures: Plan completion 88% vs 95% target. Quality metric 51.28% vs 80% target. High-risk action implementation 53.57% vs 100% target.
findings.quote: While performance remains reasonably robust in some areas, the 95% ambition for completion of the audit plan was not achieved. In addition, while there is a slight improvement in the proportion of audits receiving 'Satisfactory' assurance or better, the outcome remains significantly below the corporate target of 80%

findings.paper_title: HEAD OF INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT 2025/2026
findings.headline: Resource and capacity constraints in services are affecting consistent implementation of controls
findings.detail: Across the audit findings, several council services report facing challenges in terms of capacity and resources, which directly affect the consistent implementation of controls. This staffing and resource constraint is identified as a contributing factor to the high proportion of audits receiving Limited assurance ratings.
findings.matters: Under-resourced services cannot consistently apply financial controls and procedures, increasing fraud and error risk. For lenders, resource constraints signal the council may struggle to maintain service delivery standards or respond effectively to financial crises.
findings.figures: Resource constraints cited as reason internal audit limited follow-up work to only Limited assurance audits. 88% audit plan completion versus 95% ambition indicates audit function itself under resource pressure.
findings.quote: some services face challenges in terms of capacity and resources, which can affect the consistent implementation of controls

findings.paper_title: HEAD OF INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT 2025/2026
findings.headline: 48.71% of audits received Limited assurance, indicating systemic control environment issues
findings.detail: The paper identifies inconsistent compliance with established controls, lack of monitoring and managerial oversight in some areas, and weaknesses in the recording and documentation of processes and decisions across council services. The Head of Audit concludes these weaknesses do not undermine reasonable assurance overall, but highlight the need for sustained corporate focus on strengthening control arrangements. If not properly addressed, these issues can increase the risk that service objectives will not be effectively achieved.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on internal controls means higher risk of undetected financial irregularity, fraud, or service failure. For lenders, weak controls increase the risk profile and decrease visibility into the council's actual financial position and management quality.
findings.figures: 19 out of 43 completed audits (48.71%) received Limited assurance. Only 20 out of 39 audits with assurance levels (51.28%) obtained Satisfactory or High assurance versus corporate target of 80%.
findings.quote: 19 audits (48.71%) received 'Limited' assurance and no audit received a 'No Assurance' level

findings.headline: The council is earning 4.13% on £130.7m invested cash while paying 5.49% on £75.7m borrowed, a 136 basis point negative spread
findings.detail: Current positions show £75.7m borrowing at 5.49% average rate and £130.7m treasury investments at 4.13% average rate. This means the council is paying more for debt than it earns on cash balances — a strategy that increases annual financing costs compared to using cash to pay down debt.
findings.matters: This inefficient debt structure suggests either: (a) cash is being held for a planned purpose (major capex, reserves policy), or (b) the council has not optimised its balance sheet. Either way, it adds £0.95m+ annually to financing costs. The council's liability benchmark table indicates it held excess cash historically; this may be planned correction.
findings.figures: Borrowing £75.7m at 5.49%; investments £130.7m at 4.13%; negative spread of 136bp
findings.quote: Due to decisions taken in the past, the Council currently has £75.7m borrowing at an average interest rate of 5.49% and £130.7m treasury investments at an average rate of 4.13%

findings.headline: Treasury reserves (near-term investments) are planned to fall £86m over two years, from £141.0m to £55.0m
findings.detail: The council's readily available cash investments decline from £141.0m (2024/25 actual) to £83.5m (2025/26 forecast) to £55.0m (2026/27 budget). This £86m drawdown of liquidity over two years is substantial and indicates planned use of accumulated cash reserves to finance capital and operations.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility for unexpected costs or revenue shocks. A lender needs to understand whether this is planned and sustainable, or driven by unexpected pressures. At £55m remaining, the council still holds material reserves but the trajectory matters.
findings.figures: Near-Term Investments: 2024/25 actual £141.0m, 2025/26 forecast £83.5m, 2026/27 budget £55.0m
findings.quote: Table 9: Treasury Management Investments in £millions ... Near-Term Investments 141.0 83.5 55.0 45.0 35.0

findings.headline: External funding for capital schemes fell 73%, from £53.3m to £14.4m
findings.detail: The shift in financing shows external sources (government grants and other contributions) dropping from £53.3m in 2025/26 forecast to just £14.4m in 2026/27 budget. This suggests the end of major time-limited funding schemes. The council is shifting financing from grants toward its own resources and reduced debt.
findings.matters: Loss of external funding reflects dependence on grant cycles. A lender needs to know whether the council anticipated this decline and whether future programmes (highways, housing, levelling up schemes) have continuing funding secured.
findings.figures: External Sources 2025/26 £53.3m, 2026/27 £14.4m. Own Resources increasing from £26.4m to £16.6m; Debt decreasing from £14.4m to £9.2m
findings.quote: Table 2: Capital Financing in £ millions ... External Sources 66.5 53.3 14.4 4.9 2.5

findings.headline: Capital expenditure is planned to fall 57% in one year, from £94.1m to £40.2m, then continue falling
findings.detail: The council's capital spending budget for 2026/27 is £40.2m, down sharply from £94.1m forecast for 2025/26. The decline continues with budgets of £18.9m for 2027/28 and £8.9m for 2028/29. This represents a sustained reduction in capital investment, with 2026/27 spending less than half the prior year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this is planned programme wind-down (e.g. end of time-limited schemes like Levelling Up) or a sign of constrained financial capacity. The scale and duration of the reduction is material to assessing future service delivery and asset condition.
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the Council is planning capital expenditure of £40.2m as summarised below

findings.headline: General balances of £7.9m represent only 2.1% of the budget, tight for a council facing rising demand
findings.detail: The council's revenue reserves of £7.9m against a £379.7m budget is at the lower end of prudent policy. Against a backdrop of service demand exceeding grant growth and minimal savings headroom, this buffer is vulnerable to any service overspend or unexpected cost.
findings.matters: Low reserves limit the council's ability to absorb service shocks or one-off costs and signal reduced financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £7.9m reserves against £379,701,110 budget (2.1%)
findings.quote: The current level of the Council's general balances is £7.9m. Given the increased pressures expected on the Council's budgets over the next few years, it is considered that this level of balances will be appropriate to reserve for practical cash flow and unexpected expenditure.

findings.headline: Forecast suggests 2027/28 budget will be harder to set; no government visibility beyond May 2026
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has no forecasts for the 2027/28 local government settlement because Senedd elections are May 2026 and the incoming government is unknown. It also forecasts further pressure on balancing the 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: A lender cannot model the council's medium-term financial position; the council cannot plan. This compounds the sustainability risk of relying on council tax to close gaps year on year.
findings.figures: No settlement figures given; only forecast of increased pressure
findings.quote: Forecasts suggest there will be further pressure in aiming to set a balanced budget for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Grant increase of 4.1% falls short of the 6.5% spending rise needed to stand still
findings.detail: The council's grant increased £10.4m (4.1%), but its cost pressures from inflation, demography, and service demand total £23.1m. The gap between grant growth and spending growth has widened, not narrowed.
findings.matters: This structural mismatch—where grant growth lags cost growth—is what drives the need to raise council tax or cut services year on year. It signals unsustainability without either external funding change or service reduction.
findings.figures: Grant increase 4.1% (£10.4m); stand-still expenditure increase £23.1m (~6.5% of £356.8m base)
findings.quote: This budget is set at a time when Welsh local authorities continue to face financial challenges, where the addition to the settlement does not meet the increase in demand for services.

findings.headline: Adult and domiciliary care inflation of £2.9m, the largest single pressure on the budget
findings.detail: Within the £23.1m in total expenditure growth, £1.4m is for independent residential care homes and £1.5m for non-residential care (which includes supported housing and domiciliary care). These are not one-off costs; they are recurring.
findings.matters: Care cost inflation is a known structural pressure on councils with ageing populations and is hardest to reduce without cutting service access. This is money the council must find every year.
findings.figures: Independent Residential Care Homes £1.4m; Non-residential Care £1.5m
findings.quote: The main areas where increases are seen are: Independent Residential Care Homes £1.4m  Non-residential Care £1.5m: - Supported Housing £916k, - Domiciliary Care £301k, - Other services £281k

findings.headline: Service demand pressures of £9.9m with no savings plan to offset them
findings.detail: The council identified £9.9m in permanent additional funding needs from departmental service pressures. These are not growth—they are described as 'inevitable pressures' and include care homes and support services. The council explicitly notes that savings historically slip, and this year it has budgeted only £66k to cover those slippages.
findings.matters: Unmatched demand pressures that are being funded by tax increases rather than service changes or savings create a trajectory problem; if demand keeps rising faster than grant, the tax lever alone will not hold.
findings.figures: £9,910,580 in service bids; £66,000 savings provision for slippage
findings.quote: It is recommended that bids worth £9.9m for additional permanent resources submitted by Council departments to meet inevitable pressures on their services are approved.

findings.headline: A £115.7m funding gap closed almost entirely by council tax, not grants or savings
findings.detail: The council received a 4.1% grant increase (£10.4m) but faces £23.1m in 'stand still' expenditure needs. It has only £254k of savings available—less than a third of 1% of the budget—to contribute. The remaining gap of £115.7m will be filled by a 5.17% council tax increase, which is the only lever left.
findings.matters: Councils relying on council tax rather than grant to cover structural deficits face affordability limits and sustainability questions; this one has run out of savings to bridge the gap.
findings.figures: £115,691,720 from council tax; £264,009,390 from grant (4.1% increase); £254,140 from savings
findings.quote: Funding Gap from Council Tax and Savings 115,845,860 Less Existing Savings already approved (254,140) Funding Gap from Council Tax 115,691,720

findings.headline: Council savings schemes are experiencing delivery delays (slippages)
findings.detail: The document flags to the Governance and Audit Committee risks arising from savings slippages that require consideration before the Cabinet receives the full Savings Overview report.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings widens the budget gap and may force unplanned reserve drawdowns, service cuts, or additional borrowing
findings.figures: None provided in this document
findings.quote: consider the general risks arising from the savings slippages

findings.headline: Multiple significant corrections made to accounts during audit cycle, including £19.121m cash in transit misclassification
findings.detail: The auditor corrected seven separate categories of misstatement during the audit. The largest was £19.121m of cash in transit incorrectly recorded as creditors. Other corrections included £4.060m of misclassified creditors (short-term vs long-term), £2.141m creditor misclassified as debtor, £12.319m duplicate related party entries, and classification/presentation issues in pensions and leases notes.
findings.matters: The scale and nature of corrections indicate deficiencies in the council's initial financial close process. Large items like £19.121m being miscategorised, and £12.319m duplicate related party values, suggest gaps in reconciliation and review controls before audit testing.
findings.figures: Cash in transit misclassification: £19.121m; creditor reclassification: £4.060m; debtor/creditor swap: £2.141m; duplicate related parties: £12.319m; trade payables correction: £0.406m
findings.quote: Our audit testing identified that transactions classified as cash in transit as of 31 March 2025 were incorrectly recognised as creditors. Given that the payment instruction to the bank had been made before year end, the entity no longer held a present obligation in respect of the liability.

findings.headline: Audit fee will exceed estimate due to volume of misstatements requiring additional work
findings.detail: The auditor notes that 'due to the volume of misstatements identified during the audit, the estimated fee of £232,750 for the audit of the financial statements will be exceeded' and will liaise with the Head of Finance to agree the final additional fee. This indicates the audit required significantly more work than planned to deal with control issues and corrections.
findings.matters: Audit fee overages are a cost signal that financial reporting controls need strengthening. They also represent unplanned expenditure for the council.
findings.figures: Budgeted audit fee: £232,750; actual fee to be higher (amount not yet determined)
findings.quote: Due to the volume of misstatements identified during the audit, the estimated fee of £232,750 for the audit of the financial statements will be exceeded. We will liaise with the Head of Finance to agree the final additional fee.

findings.headline: Statutory audit deadline cannot be met — accounts will be certified 19 November instead of 31 October
findings.detail: The auditor confirms the accounts will be certified on 19 November 2025, more than two weeks after the statutory deadline of 31 October. The report attributes this to the timing of the Committee meeting (13 November) rather than accounting delays, but notes that next year's audit window will be shorter and 'similar delays could pose a significant risk to meeting the revised certification deadline of 30 September'.
findings.matters: Missing statutory deadlines raises governance and transparency concerns for lenders assessing timeliness of financial reporting. The auditor's warning about next year's tighter deadline suggests the council is cutting it close on audit completion.
findings.figures: Actual certification: 19 November 2025; statutory deadline: 31 October 2025 (19 days late)
findings.quote: We are aiming to certify your accounts on 19 November 2025 following approval of the accounts at the Governance and Audit Committee on 13 November 2025. This falls after the statutory deadline of 31 October, which could not be met due to the timing of the Committee meeting.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 leases implementation incomplete with system limitations preventing proper accounting treatment
findings.detail: Auditor identified multiple non-compliances with IFRS 16 requirements. Peppercorn leases were not revalued at fair value; lessor arrangements involving sub-leases were not properly assessed for control; a retrospective adjustment was made when prospective application is required. The council's fixed asset system cannot reclassify assets from PPE to Right of Use Assets, preventing £1.531m being recorded correctly. The leases note required complete redrafting for CIPFA compliance.
findings.matters: Incomplete implementation of a major accounting standard affects asset valuation accuracy on the balance sheet. The system limitation means errors cannot be corrected, indicating infrastructure weakness that could affect future financial reporting.
findings.figures: £1.531m cannot be reclassified; peppercorn lease valuation error £0.675m; retrospective adjustment of £0.997m
findings.quote: Audit testing identified that the Right of Use Assets of peppercorn leases had not been revalued at fair value in accordance with IFRS 16 - Leases guidance... one asset was valued at £0.675 million. This asset should have been recognised as a Right of Use Asset on the Balance Sheet, resulting in an understatement of £0.675 million.

findings.headline: Seven uncorrected misstatements left in accounts, totalling material amounts, with council accepting them as immaterial
findings.detail: The auditor identified multiple misstatements during testing but the council has chosen not to correct them. These include PPE overstated by £0.332m, capital expenditure tracking issues of £0.775m and £1.225m, asset valuation errors of £0.408m, a 12-year-old creditor of £0.907m still on balance sheet, lease accounting gaps of £0.675m and £1.531m, and a £0.997m retrospective adjustment that doesn't comply with IFRS 16. The auditor has accepted these as immaterial but requests written reasons for non-correction.
findings.matters: The quantity and nature of uncorrected misstatements indicate control weaknesses in accounting processes and financial reporting. A lender would question whether the financial position is accurately presented and whether the council's finance team has sufficient control over its accounts.
findings.figures: PPE £0.332m overstatement; capital expenditure £0.775m and £1.225m; asset valuation £0.408m; creditor balance £0.907m; lease understatement £0.675m; sub-lease reclassification £1.531m; lease retrospective adjustment £0.997m
findings.quote: We set out below the misstatements we identified in the accounts, which has been discussed with management but remains uncorrected. We request that these misstatements be corrected. If you decide not to correct these misstatements, we ask that you provide us with the reasons in writing for not correcting them.

findings.headline: Council tax inflation of 9.54% in 2024/25 is contributing to collection difficulties and taxpayer affordability issues
findings.detail: Council tax increased by 9.54% in 2024/25, one of the highest increases in recent years (prior years ranged 2.95%-4.95%). This substantial increase is cited in the report as a contributing factor to both the reduced collection rate and taxpayer ability to pay.
findings.matters: High inflation in an essential service charge reduces households' ability to pay, directly contributing to the documented collection rate decline and affecting cash flow across the council area
findings.quote: with an inflation increase of 9.54% in 2024/25. Therefore, this may also have been a contributing factor to the reduction in the collection rate and the financial ability of the taxpayers to pay their bills.

findings.headline: Self-catering property transfers to council tax with 150% premiums and backdated bills are creating substantial unpaid debts
findings.detail: 692 properties transferred from non-domestic rates to council tax in 2024/25, with 558 in the second half of the year. These transfers carried 150% council tax premiums and bills backdated to April 2023, creating substantial amounts that remained unpaid at year-end. Further transfers are occurring (395 by end September 2025 vs 134 in same period 2024) and Welsh Government rule changes may increase this further.
findings.matters: Large backdated bills with high premiums create unpaid debt that swells the £8.2m outstanding figure; expected further transfers mean this collection problem will persist and potentially worsen in coming years
findings.figures: 692 properties transferred in 2024/25 (558 in second half); 395 transferred by end September 2025 (compared to 134 in same period 2024)
findings.quote: In 2024/25, 692 properties were transferred back to Council Tax...to the Council Tax band where they needed to pay the basic council tax and 150% council tax premium. They were also applications that were being backdated and some of them back to April 2023.

findings.headline: Email backlog of 3,500 messages created months of delays in responding to taxpayers, contributing to collection decline
findings.detail: A backlog of over three months in responding to taxpayer emails meant households were getting into arrears before receiving bills or setting up payment arrangements. While reduced to 185 messages by November 2025, this backlog significantly contributed to the 2024/25 collection rate decline and delay in sending reminders.
findings.matters: Service failures in basic taxpayer administration (responding to enquiries) directly contributed to documented collection rate decline and indicate operational weaknesses in critical revenue-generating functions
findings.figures: Email backlog: 3,500 messages at start of 2025/26, reduced to 185 by November 2025
findings.quote: A backlog of over three months in responding to emails from taxpayers which meant that many of them were getting into a situation of arrears even before their bills were received, due to a delay in receiving the bill or a delay in setting up payment/direct debit arrangements.

findings.headline: Second homes and empty property premiums have significantly lower collection rates at 87.29% and 81.41%
findings.detail: Collection performance on accounts with property premiums is substantially weaker than basic council tax. Second homes premium accounts collect only 87.29% (£3.1m outstanding) and empty property premium accounts only 81.41% (£0.8m outstanding), compared to 95.09% on basic council tax only accounts. These premiums account for £3.9m of the total £8.2m debt.
findings.matters: A structural collection weakness on a specific category of accounts represents a persistent revenue problem; the £3.9m shortfall on premiums alone is substantial and the backlog has existed since the premium's introduction in 2018
findings.figures: Premium accounts: 87.29% collection (second homes, £3.1m outstanding), 81.41% collection (empty property, £0.8m outstanding); Basic council tax only: 95.09%
findings.quote: It can be seen from the table above that our overall collection rates are affected by the second home and empty property premium, with the debts on accounts that include a premium in addition to the basic tax at £3.9m (£3.1m second homes and £0.8m empty properties)

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate of 92.9% is the lowest among 22 Welsh councils
findings.detail: Gwynedd collected only 92.9% of council tax due in 2024/25, compared to the Welsh highest of 97.7% and the second-worst council at 94.1%. The collection rate has declined from 94.4% in 2023/24. This leaves £8.2m of outstanding debts out of £116.5m due.
findings.matters: Council tax is fundamental revenue for service delivery and financial stability; collecting below Welsh peers raises creditworthiness concerns and indicates a 7% revenue shortfall affecting the council's financial position
findings.figures: 92.9% collection rate (2024/25), down from 94.4% (2023/24); Welsh highest 97.7%; £8.2m outstanding debts out of £116.5m due
findings.quote: Council Tax collection rates (within the year) in Gwynedd were the lowest in Wales in 2024/25, with 92.9% of debts collected by the end of the financial year on 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: The council plans to use one-off reserves to balance 2026/27, with explicit warning this creates financial viability risk.
findings.detail: The council states it cannot leave the £14.9m gap unaddressed and will use 'one-off reserve funds for the rest' after permanent savings. It then explicitly warns that using £5m in reserves would cause the 2027/28 gap to jump to £17.3m (from £12.3m forecast), creating 'a significant financial viability risk.' The council's own analysis recognises that reserve drawdowns are self-defeating in a multi-year deficit.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion accelerates financial distress; reserves are the essential buffer against operational shocks. The council's acknowledgement of this cascading risk is itself a material warning for lenders monitoring financial covenants.
findings.figures: £14.9m 2026/27 gap; if £5m covered by reserves, 2027/28 gap rises to £17.3m from £12.3m forecast.
findings.quote: if we were planning to set a balanced budget this year using £5 million of one-off reserves, it would mean that our gap in 2027/28 would increase from the current £12.3 million to £17.3 million and create a significant financial viability risk

findings.headline: After 15 years of finding £74 million in savings, the council states it cannot cut further without direct impact on residents.
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that it has 'reached a point where we cannot squeeze more of it without cutting services that would have a clear and direct impact on the residents of Gwynedd.' Services are already under pressure with unavoidable overspending occurring due to insufficient budgets. This signals the end of efficiency-driven savings and the onset of service reduction.
findings.matters: Future deficit reductions will require genuine service cuts rather than efficiency gains, making them harder to implement and more politically contentious. This increases execution risk for any deficit-reduction programme.
findings.figures: £74 million in savings over 15 years; projected savings declining to £0.3m (2026/27), £0.1m (2027/28), and £0 (2028/29).
findings.quote: we have now reached a point where we cannot squeeze more of it without cutting services that would have a clear and direct impact on the residents of Gwynedd

findings.headline: A £40 million structural budget gap over three years with no confirmed funding pathway to close it.
findings.detail: Gwynedd faces budget deficits of £14.9m in 2026/27, £12.3m in 2027/28, and £12.8m in 2028/29. Pay and price inflation account for £20m, £17.4m, and £17.8m in annual spending pressures respectively, while expected funding increases total only £4.8m to £5m per year. The council has no definitive plan to address the gap without significant service cuts, Council Tax increases, or reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: A structural budget deficit signals the council cannot sustain current service levels and debt obligations without material changes to funding or spending, directly affecting financial viability and debt repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £40 million cumulative gap; £14.9 million 2026/27; £12.3 million 2027/28; £12.8 million 2028/29. Pay inflation £9.3m, £8m, £8.3m respectively. Price inflation £4.7m, £3.9m, £4m respectively.
findings.quote: cumulative gap of £40 million is projected over three years

news_drafts.headline: North Wales CJC forecasts £39,874 net overspend for 2026/27, with £516,625 on unbudgeted consultants
news_drafts.lead:
The North Wales Corporate Joint Committee (CJC) expects to end 2026/27 with a net overspend of £39,874, according to its July review report before the Governance and Audit Sub-committee on 15 October. The extra cost will be met from reserves, the money the body has set aside, on top of a £624,590 transfer already approved.

The small net figure sits on a larger movement in gross spending. Budgeted expenditure of £1,959,770 is forecast to reach £2,589,644, an overspend of £629,874, or 32%. The main driver is £516,625 on external consultants, against a budget of nothing: £254,400 for programme management, £236,225 for legal work and £26,000 for business advisers. Spending on supplies and services is also forecast to be £435,864 above budget.

Reserves stood at £1,636,007 on 31 March 2026 and are estimated at £971,543 by 31 March 2027. The CJC's statutory finance officer says reserves are expected to be needed for future budgets, as the CJC's resourcing requirements increase and future grants have not been confirmed.

news_drafts.headline: Gwynedd has £16m of new capital money against £19.76m of requests, and built 118 homes against 247
news_drafts.lead:
Gwynedd Council's Cabinet has been told it has about £16m in additional money for capital spending (spending on things that last, such as buildings and flood defences) but requests from education and flood prevention projects come to £19.76m, a gap of £3.76m. The council's Capital Strategy says: "Given that there is currently £16M of additional resource available, it is not possible to fund everything and therefore, there will be a need to prioritise."

The £16m has built up since the council approved its 2024-2034 Asset Plan. It comes from capital grants, receipts, and £3.5m released by de-committing the Health and Care Hub project. The papers do not say which schemes will be funded or dropped.

A separate report to the meeting, the Annual Monitoring Report, covers housing. It records 118 homes completed in the Gwynedd Planning Authority area in 2025/26. That is 129 fewer than the annual average requirement of 247 (52.2% below) and 107 fewer than the forecast trajectory of 225. Since the local plan was adopted in 2017, 2,805 homes have been completed against a trajectory of 3,712, which is 24.4% below.

news_drafts.headline: Gwynedd took out no new loans in first quarter of 2026/27, leaving borrowing at £73.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Gwynedd Council took out no new loans in the first quarter of 2026/27, and its total borrowing stood at £73.9m, unchanged from 31 March. The figures are in the treasury management update (the report on how the council borrows and invests its spare cash) that went to its Governance and Audit Committee on 29 September.

The council says this is deliberate. It is using what is known as internal borrowing, meaning it pays for long-lasting spending from its own cash rather than taking a loan. This saves interest but uses up the cash cushion. The paper says the approach keeps borrowing below the council's underlying need.

The paper says the strategy "enabled the Council to reduce net borrowing costs (despite foregoing investment income) and reduce overall treasury risk". In other words, cash that is spent in place of a loan no longer earns interest as an investment, but the council judges the interest it saves on loans to be worth more. Its net investments stood at £11.4m.
